title: The Emperor's Lost Hunting Falcon (ES)
summary: Akbar's prized hunting falcon escapes into a tall tree and refuses to return. Courtiers throw stones in vain, but Birbal coaxes the bird with gentle love.
full_text:
During an imperial hunt in the dense forests of Bharatpur, Emperor Akbar's favorite hunting falcon—a magnificent white bird named Shahin, trained for five years—took flight after a pheasant, broke its silk jesses, and flew to the topmost branch of a colossal hundred-foot banyan tree.

The falcon sat high upon the branch, preening its feathers, refusing to descend.

Akbar was desperate: 'My falcon is irreplaceable! Call the bird down!'

The royal falconers blew silver whistles, waved leather lures, and shouted commands, but the bird remained perched high in the sky.

Impatience seized the imperial guards: two archers proposed shooting blunt arrows near the bird to startle it, and courtiers threw stones into the branches, but the stones merely terrified the falcon, causing it to hop even higher onto a precarious bough!

Akbar was on the verge of tears.

Birbal stepped forward: 'Sire, command the soldiers to drop their stones and whistles. Violence and loud shouts will only drive the bird to fly away into the mountains.'

Birbal asked everyone to retreat fifty paces and sit quietly in the grass in absolute silence.

Birbal took a wooden bowl filled with fresh, cool well water and a strip of tender, raw quail meat.

Walking alone to the base of the tree, Birbal sat down quietly upon the mossy roots, placed the water bowl on the grass, and held the fresh meat in his open, motionless palm.

Birbal did not shout. He did not whistle. He simply sat motionless, breathing calmly, humming a soft, rhythmic lullaby that the falconers had sung to the bird when it was a fledgling.

For twenty minutes, absolute peace reigned in the clearing.

High above, the thirsty, hungry falcon looked down. It saw no stones flying, heard no angry shouts, and saw the cool water and fresh meat held in an open, gentle hand.

Slowly, gracefully, the white falcon spread its wings, glided down through the green leaves in a silent spiral, and alighted softly upon Birbal's open wrist, drinking eagerly from the water bowl!

Birbal gently secured the silk jesses and carried the bird to Emperor Akbar.

Akbar embraced his minister with overflowing joy: 'Birbal, you retrieved with gentle patience what fifty shouting men could not achieve with stones!'

Birbal smiled: 'Sire, whether dealing with birds, children, or rebellious subjects, fear drives them away, but patience, peace, and nourishment invariably bring them safely home.'
